column1: Early incretin research showed that oral glucose stimulates more insulin release than intravenous glucose. <citations>bbhfiucw:3</citations>
Scientists isolated active glp-1 and demonstrated its ability to stimulate insulin and suppress glucagon. <citations>pg265-fa:2</citations>
Human studies established that glp-1 could lower blood glucose in people with type 2 diabetes. <citations>pg265-fa:4</citations>
Understanding glp-1 degradation enabled dpp-4 inhibitors and longer-lasting glp-1 medicines. <citations>pg265-fa:5</citations>
Exenatide became the first approved glp-1 receptor agonist, translating incretin research into diabetes treatment. <citations>de8wmlxw:7</citations>
Molecular engineering extended drug action, enabling practical daily and weekly injectable treatments. <citations>ya7v3tra:4,sfjk3u6g:5</citations>
Appetite and weight-loss benefits expanded glp-1 medicines into approved obesity treatment. <citations>ya7v3tra:8</citations>
Oral semaglutide brought glp-1 treatment beyond injections to tablet-based delivery. <citations>sfjk3u6g:5</citations>
Outcomes trials established cardiovascular and kidney benefits for selected glp-1 therapies and patient populations. <citations>6odgfy7q:10,12,15-16</citations>
Dual- and triple-receptor agonists broadened glp-1–based development toward greater weight loss and metabolic benefit. <citations>sfjk3u6g:8</citations>
